"As of today, my position is no because that's what my constituents and my community is saying," said Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) when asked if she backed Jeffries, "It's really about the process. items.title: Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces
items.summary:
Justice Clarence Thomas warned Monday that the Supreme Court is leaving the door open for states to compel speech from private citizens by not taking up a challenge to a California law.

On Monday, the Supreme Court declined a petition to hear a case from a California physician who argued that the state government was forcing her to make statements she disagreed with while teaching a mandatory course for doctors. Thomas was joined by Justice Samuel Alito in dissenting from the decision, arguing that allowing the law to stand could have implications reaching far beyond the medical field.

The case stems from California’s requirement that all its licensed physicians complete 50 hours of state-approved continuing education courses every two years. California requires continuing medical education courses to include instruction on implicit bias, either through examples of how it affects physicians' treatment decisions and health outcomes or strategies for addressing how those biases may contribute to healthcare disparities.

items.title: Trump brings two divided Cabinet heavyweights to China as controversy hangs over high-stakes talks
items.summary:
President Donald Trump is bringing two powerful Cabinet officials divided over restrictions on China's access to advanced American AI chips on his high-stakes Asia trip, as controversy over the issue follows them into talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are both accompanying Trump on the four-day trip despite reports of a dispute over whether to blacklist a company suspected of helping China obtain restricted American AI technology. Trump acknowledged their competing views Monday and suggested Lutnick may have delayed action to avoid worsening relations with Beijing.

"He might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have if you didn't delay it. If you didn't do something, you could have a blow up with China. We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides," the president said.

The dispute follows reports that Lutnick resisted efforts to place Singapore-based Megaspeed on a U.S. trade blacklist, despite Trump reportedly supporting action against the company on three occasions this year, according to Axios. Megaspeed has faced allegations that its operations helped Chinese companies gain access to restricted Nvidia chips.

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation, scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold, the leisure centres closed, the mental health services for…

items.title: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace
items.summary:
The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe

So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser.

For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are.

Continue reading...
items.t: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace

The secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.

This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.

items.title: The Democratic party is at a critical crossroad. Can it do the right thing? | Osita Nwanevu
items.summary:
Americans are at a real point of decision – not election day, but this heady, uncertain moment after

Until 2026, the most important midterm year of the last quarter-century was very probably 2010. Barack Obama famously called the elections a “shellacking” for the Democratic party and he was right. Thanks to a sluggish economic recovery from the Great Recession and backlash against the passage of the Affordable Care Act, Republicans took control of the House with a 63-seat gain – the largest House sweep since the 1940s – and won six seats in the Senate.

But the 2010 midterms were significant well beyond those numbers. It was the first election shaped by the rise of the Tea Party and its blend of rightwing economic populism and xenophobia. Those aligned with the movement lost nearly twice the number of races they won, but the presence of an energized hard-right contingent among Republicans in Congress shaped legislative outcomes for the remainder of Obama’s term and beyond.

items.title: Prep for disaster, ministers said – and millions stocked up. It’s the UK government that’s not ready | Jean Coussins
items.summary:
Telling people to set aside food, water and cash is all very well, but we need a truly joined-up resilience strategy – and we don’t have one

  • Jean Coussins is chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee

The public has been stocking up on bottled water, tinned food and wind-up radios since the government launched its Be Ready campaign last month. But it’s not the public’s willingness to prepare that should worry us. What’s missing is the government’s willingness to provide candid information about the escalating nature and frequency of the threats we face, and a coherent resilience plan that can be activated from the top of government to local, community and household levels.

In July, the then security minister, Angela Eagle, admitted to the House of Lords national resilience committee, of which I am chair, that the government did not want to “frighten people”. But shielding the public from uncomfortable realities risks leaving them ill prepared for the very emergencies they need to withstand.

Jean Coussins is an independent crossbench peer and chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee

Long before national political leaders and media were paying any attention, long before the Louisiana v Callais supreme court decision gutted the Voting Rights Act, Mississippi organizers were working to grow political participation and improve quality of life in a state that often ranks low on its residents’ health and wellbeing.

Activists’ momentum contributed to Democrat Scott Colom’s historic upset in the midterm elections. A loose coalition of about a dozen, mostly Black-led nonprofits or initiatives rallied residents after Callais, the April decision that set off a flurry of redistricting efforts across southern states. That case was not the sole impetus for organizing efforts across Mississippi, but it turned out thousands in the 20 May “Mississippi Fights Back” rally. Callais became the most recent opportunity to channel people’s frustrations and hopes into action – and to harness previous campaigns that go back years and even decades.

City has failed to build infrastructure that could reduce threat, and saw 400 fires, 83 injuries and 12 deaths this year

Fires from lithium-ion batteries, which power ebikes and scooters, have become regular occurrences in New York, causing deaths and fear among residents, but the city has failed to build infrastructure that could reduce the threat.

New York has seen a dramatic uptick this year in fires from the batteries. In 2025, there were 292 fires, 51 injuries and one death, according to the New York fire department (FDNY). This year, there have already been more than 400 fires, 83 injuries and 12 deaths.

The election for Democratic Senate leader between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen must be understood for what it is.

This is not a personality contest. This is a debate about the future of the Democratic party. It is a debate about whether the Democratic party remains a top-down party dominated by billionaire campaign contributors, inside-the-beltway consultants and 30-second TV ads, or whether we can transform it into a grassroots party of, by and for the working families of our country.

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s wake of destruction at the Pentagon – Stateside with Kai and Carter
items.summary:
Pete Hegseth has managed to dodge an impeachment trial, for the second time. And Republicans have avoided — for now — a major public accounting of the damage done at the Pentagon during Hegseth’s tenure. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment detail charges that are likely to return when Democrats take the majority next year. Kai Wright speaks with Guardian senior political enterprise reporter Aram Roston about how people inside the military have reacted to the impeachment and to Hegseth’s tenure, from the boat strikes in the Caribbean to the massive loss of experienced leadership and a dramatic depletion of munitions in Iran. Roston, who has covered the Pentagon across several administrations, describes a Pentagon shaken up in ways he’s never before seen.
